paras: The lynching of Caleb Campbell took place on the night of June 2, 1882, when about eighty disguised riders took Campbell, a Black man, from the jail at Winnsboro, South Carolina, and hanged him from a tree three miles outside town. Campbell was being held for trial on a charge of attempting to assault a white woman near Blythewood in Fairfield County. A coroner's jury found that he had been murdered by persons unknown, and the Winnsboro newspaper published an editorial defending the lynching.

According to the News and Courier's Winnsboro correspondent, Mrs. Martha Rains was seized and thrown to the ground at a spring near her house near Blythewood on the evening of May 24 by a man who fled after a struggle; she later identified Campbell as her attacker. That account says an approaching wagon frightened him away; the Columbia Register credited her resistance, saying she bit his hands.

Trial Justice Hogan committed Campbell after a preliminary examination to await the Court of Sessions, which was to open the following Monday. Because of "many threats of lynching," he was taken to the Winnsboro jail by train under a special constable.

Between midnight and one o'clock on the night of Friday, June 2, the riders came into Winnsboro, posted pickets, and called the sheriff to the jail door with a story that they had a prisoner to deliver. In the News and Courier's version, several men threw the sheriff to the floor and took the cell key from his pockets; the Columbia Register said Sheriff McCarley gave up the keys at revolver point. They forced Campbell's cell, handcuffed him, put a rope around his neck and set him on a mule.

The party rode at a gallop down the Columbia road to a large post oak about three miles below the town, threw the rope over a limb, and led the mule out from under him. The correspondent wrote that the men wore masks, blackened faces or sheets and worked "with military precision," riding away so quietly that many townspeople did not wake. A placard pinned to Campbell's clothing read, "Our mothers, wives and sisters shall be protected, even with our lives."

At the inquest held by Coroner George S. Hinnant the next day, before about a hundred people, the jury found Campbell "killed and murdered by hanging by some person or persons to the jury unknown." No report of arrests, indictments or a trial of the lynchers appears in the coverage. His friends made no demand for the body, which was buried in a county coffin just under the limb where he died; a member of St. Mark's Baptist Church, a Black congregation, had objected to burial in its churchyard.

The correspondent said the Black people at the inquest "did not exhibit any feeling." He also wrote that Campbell "bore a bad character" and that Mrs. Rains was in critical condition after a premature birth.

The first notice was a News and Courier special telegraphed from Charleston on June 3, which ran the next day in Richmond, Memphis, New York and Rock Island, under headlines such as "Hanged by a Disguised Mob" and, in Savannah, "A Negro Fiend Lynched." The woman's name drifted in transmission to Rainson, Paines, Kains and Rams, and one Vermont summary said Campbell was lynched "for raping a white woman," though every detailed account described an attempt.

In South Carolina, the Abbeville Press and Banner and the Winnsboro Fairfield News and Herald reprinted the News and Courier letter, and the Yorkville Enquirer reprinted the Columbia Register's "Judge Lynch in Fairfield," which said "Judge Lynch's Court" had heard the evidence. The Fairfield News and Herald defended the lynching in an editorial titled "The Higher Law," calling this the one case in which lynch law was justifiable even though the crime "was not consummated," and warning that any "white beast or the black beast" who struck at virtue would "swing."

The two local accounts differ on who cut down the body: the News and Courier, whose correspondent reported the inquest testimony, says the sheriff and Major T. W. Woodward did, while the Columbia Register says the lynchers cut Campbell down and left him under the tree.

bases: A party of about eighty disguised men took Campbell, held for trial on an assault charge, from the Winnsboro jail and hanged him (A12, A14, A16).

About eighty masked men overpowered the sheriff, took Campbell from jail and hanged him; the coroner's jury found he was 'killed and murdered' by persons unknown (A12, A14, A16). The mob acted on the accusation of attempted assault on a white woman, and its placard and the local editorial framed the act as protection and 'higher law' (A13, A14).

The News and Courier correspondent's letter (A12, A14) and the Columbia Register's separate account (A16) agree on the taking from jail, the hanging below town and the inquest verdict, as does the wire (A5).

accounts.gist: Eighty riders told the sheriff they had a prisoner, seized him when he opened the door, took the key from his pockets, and hanged Campbell from a post oak three miles out; the sheriff and Major Woodward cut the body down.

accounts.label: Columbia Register
accounts.gist: Two or three men summoned Sheriff McCarley, then a large force demanded the keys at revolver point; the party hanged Campbell three and a half miles below town, cut him down and left him, and the sheriff found him there.

accounts.label: Charleston wire
accounts.gist: Disguised men gained admittance by a stratagem, overpowered the sheriff and hanged Campbell about three miles from Winnsboro; the sheriff pursued too late.

accounts.label: Coroner's jury
accounts.gist: Campbell was killed and murdered by hanging by persons unknown.

framing.detail: The Fairfield News and Herald's editorial 'The Higher Law' called the case the one in which lynch law is justifiable and warned that any 'beast' who 'strikes at virtue' would swing.
The News and Courier letter opened 'One of the most fiendish outrages ever committed in Fairfield county has been terribly avenged' and said Campbell 'fully merited the justice' done him.
The wire ran under headlines such as 'A Negro Fiend Lynched' and 'Lynching of an Alleged South Carolina Criminal' from Savannah to Rock Island.
Northern and church news summaries gave a line each, one stating as fact that he was lynched 'for raping a white woman'.
